{"id": "2:132/q04", "question": "Why does Abraham address his sons?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q04/p1", "position": "A father's special care and his sons' readiness make them fitting recipients; addressing all of them shows the religion's priority.", "reasons": "Jishumī and Ṭabrisī say he also invited everyone; Rāzī says no son was excluded and no other bequest competed with religion. Abū Ḥayyān says the sons already followed Islam, so the counsel seeks their afterlife safety, is unrestricted in time and place, and ends with a strong warning. Bursevī says a sound leader's family helps make the community sound; he and Rāzī note the urgency of a father’s care."}, {"id": "2:132/q04/p2", "position": "He passed on a precious religion to successors so they would not deviate from it.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says people of truth guard hard-won teaching through succession; Biqāʿī notes that descendants transmitted the testament in turn, especially Jacob."}]}
{"id": "2:132/q05", "question": "How many sons of Abraham are reported, and who were they?", "turns_on": "Different transmitted genealogical counts and lists.", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q05/p1", "position": "Four sons are counted, including Ishmael, Isaac, Midian and Mada'in/Medan.", "reasons": "Muqātil counts four in the opening note; Ibn al-Jawzī names them, and Elmalılı repeats the four-name list as one report."}, {"id": "2:132/q05/p2", "position": "Eight sons are counted: Ishmael, Isaac, and six by Qantura/Keturah.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī, Baghawī, Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān, Bursevī and Ibn ʿĀshūr name the mothers Hagar, Sarah, and Qantura. Lists of six vary (Midian, Midan, Zamran and other forms); Qurṭubī says Qantura married Abraham after Sarah's death. Ibn ʿĀshūr says only Midian's line receives much Torah detail, including Moses' refuge and Jethro/Reuel; Abū Ḥayyān says only Ishmael and Isaac left enduring lines."}, {"id": "2:132/q05/p3", "position": "Other counts are fourteen, twelve, or twenty-four sons.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī lists fourteen beside four and eight; Ālūsī attributes a twelve-son list to al-Itqān, while Elmalılı reports twenty-four. Al-Itqān names the twelve as Ismail, Ishaq, Madyan, Zamran, Sarh, Nafsh, Nafshan, Umaym, Kaysan, Surah, Lutan, and Nafish."}]}
{"id": "2:132/q06", "question": "What background is given about Ishmael and Isaac?", "turns_on": "Different age and sacrifice reports in the historical background.", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q06/p1", "position": "Ishmael was Hagar's son, older than Isaac, and was taken to Mecca as an infant.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī prefers infancy over reported ages two and fourteen; historians cited by Abū Ḥayyān say he was fourteen years older than Isaac and eighty-nine when Abraham died. Qurṭubī gives Ishmael's death at 137 or 130, Isaac's at 180, and says Isaac was buried beside Abraham; Abū Ḥayyān concurs on the latter. Qurṭubī lists Isaac's descendants as Romans, Greeks, Armenians and Israelites."}, {"id": "2:132/q06/p2", "position": "Reports put Ishmael at two or fourteen when brought to Mecca.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī transmits both reported ages and separately favors infancy."}, {"id": "2:132/q06/p3", "position": "The son offered for sacrifice was Ishmael.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī reports this identification while favoring the Isaac identification."}, {"id": "2:132/q06/p4", "position": "The son offered for sacrifice was Isaac.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī calls this the more correct identification and says he will discuss it under al-Ṣāffāt."}]}
{"id": "2:132/q07", "question": "How is Abraham's name read or adapted?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q07/p1", "position": "Ibrāhāmu is a canonical pronunciation with long ā in the final syllable.", "reasons": "Qirāʾāt-ER says the adaptation affects pronunciation and lineage resonance rather than syntax; Ibn Khālawayh notes Arabic adaptation of foreign names."}]}
{"id": "2:132/q08", "question": "How does وَيَعْقُوبُ attach to the sentence, and who receives the counsel?", "turns_on": "The case of Yaʿqūb and whether coordination, ellipsis, or object attachment governs him.", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q08/p1", "position": "Nominative Jacob is coordinated with Abraham: each charged his own sons.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī rejects making the two patriarchs' charges different; Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda report the shared testament. Ṭabrisī and Samin prefer coordination because it needs no ellipsis; Naḥḥās explicitly parses both as nominative subjects. Ibn Kathīr cites the next account at 2:133 for Jacob's own charge."}, {"id": "2:132/q08/p2", "position": "Nominative Jacob begins a new clause with an understood 'he charged' or 'he said'; his own sons then hear the address.", "reasons": "Akhfash prefers this analysis because Abraham's earlier clause already implies speech. Jishumī, Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān and Samin report it; Samin notes that on this parse the quoted 'my sons' belongs to Jacob."}, {"id": "2:132/q08/p3", "position": "Accusative Jacob is coordinated with 'his sons' and was among those Abraham enjoined, as a grandson.", "reasons": "Akhfash offers object coordination; ʿAmr b. Fāʾid and Ismāʿīl b. ʿAbd Allāh are named as readers. Abū Ḥayyān says 'sons' can include a grandson. Qushayrī objects that Jacob was neither a son nor alive to hear it; Ibn Kathīr disputes the chronological objection using 11:71, 29:27 and 21:72."}, {"id": "2:132/q08/p4", "position": "Jacob is an implicit agent of the enjoining.", "reasons": "Ālūsī records this analysis only to call it remote."}]}
{"id": "2:132/q09", "question": "How is the name Yaʿqūb explained?", "turns_on": "Whether an Arabic birth/descendant etymology can apply to a foreign proper name.", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q09/p1", "position": "He was named for following his twin Esau out of the womb while holding Esau's heel.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is repeatedly cited. Bursevī adds a womb dialogue: Esau demanded to emerge first; Jacob yielded for their mother's safety, and their dispositions later diverged. Qurṭubī and Ālūsī doubt the etymology or report; Samin argues a foreign proper name cannot be derived as though Arabic."}, {"id": "2:132/q09/p2", "position": "The name relates to Jacob's many descendants.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī and Baghawī report this alternative; Samin rejects Arabic derivations of the foreign name."}, {"id": "2:132/q09/p3", "position": "It is an indeclinable foreign proper name, though yaʿqūb also names a partridge in Arabic.", "reasons": "Samin argues that a masculine name derived from the Arabic bird would decline; Qurṭubī says the foreign name only coincides with the bird name."}]}
{"id": "2:132/q10", "question": "What is reported about Jacob, his sons, and their lives?", "turns_on": "The biographical reports and the chronology relevant to Jacob hearing Abraham's counsel.", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q10/p1", "position": "Jacob instructed twelve sons, the tribal ancestors, and later died in Egypt with burial in Canaan beside Isaac.", "reasons": "Sources list the twelve sons by name. Qurṭubī and Bursevī give Jacob 147 years and Joseph's transfer of his body; Ibn ʿĀshūr names Rebekah as his mother, Israel as his other name and Machpelah as the burial site. Bursevī adds that Esau and Jacob died the same day and were buried together."}, {"id": "2:132/q10/p2", "position": "Jacob gathered his sons after seeing Egyptians worship idols, fire, and cattle.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī reports this as the setting for his question about what they would worship after him; Bursevī repeats the Egyptian idolatry background."}, {"id": "2:132/q10/p3", "position": "Jacob lived in Abraham's lifetime.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr cites the promise of Isaac and Jacob at 11:71 and grants of Jacob in 29:27 and 21:72; he also discusses Jerusalem's building and a forty-year interval from the Sacred Mosque, rejecting Ibn Ḥibbān's chronology. Ibn ʿĀshūr agrees."}, {"id": "2:132/q10/p4", "position": "Jacob was born only after Abraham died.", "reasons": "Qushayrī, as quoted by Qurṭubī and Ibn Kathīr, uses this against the accusative reading; Ibn Kathīr says this requires sound proof."}]}
{"id": "2:132/q11", "question": "How does يَٰبَنِىَّ introduce the testament, and what is its reading?", "turns_on": "Whether the speech after the testament requires an implied saying verb or is governed by the speech sense of enjoining; a variant supplies an.", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q11/p1", "position": "An implied verb of saying introduces the quoted address.", "reasons": "Basran grammarians require 'he said' because a full sentence cannot normally be a direct object; Akhfash and Naḥḥās offer this. If Jacob is accusative the implied verb is singular, while nominative allows dual, according to Ālūsī. Farra, Ṭabarī, Thaʿlabī, Jishumī and others compare Qur'anic speech constructions, including 4:11 and 33:29."}, {"id": "2:132/q11/p2", "position": "No separate saying verb is needed because enjoining itself is a speech act.", "reasons": "Kufans connect the quotation directly to waṣṣā; al-Ṭabarī treats omitted an as semantic syntax, illustrated by 4:11 and poetry. Al-Farrāʾ rejects the claim that an was intended and elided: such speech clauses may appear with or without it."}, {"id": "2:132/q11/p3", "position": "Ubayy, Ibn Masʿūd and al-Ḍaḥḥāk read 'an yā banī' with an explicit explanatory particle.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, Thaʿlabī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān, Samin and Ālūsī cite the reading. Samin says it supports an explanatory clause rather than a verbal noun; those denying explanatory an call it redundant. Ālūsī notes that it can remove Basrans' need for an implied verb."}]}
{"id": "2:132/q12", "question": "What is the vocative and possessive form of يَٰبَنِىَّ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q12/p1", "position": "It means 'O my sons'; the possessive yāʾ is opened to avoid two consecutive quiescent letters.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās compares 14:22; Qurṭubī transmits his explanation. {"id": "2:132/q13", "question": "Why say 'my sons' in the address?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q13/p1", "position": "The tender kinship address encourages acceptance of the chosen religion.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says it stirs them to Islam and makes departure from God's chosen way irrational."}]}
{"id": "2:132/q14", "question": "Why does إِنَّ take kasra here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q14/p1", "position": "It starts the quoted speech conveyed by waṣṣā/awṣā, either directly or after an implicit 'he said.'", "reasons": "Zajjāj, Abū Isḥāq and Ibn ʿAṭiyya explain the kasra by reported speech. Naḥḥās and Qurṭubī allow an omitted speech verb. The Basran/Kufan analyses of the vocative apply to the ensuing quotation."}]}
{"id": "2:132/q15", "question": "What does ٱصْطَفَىٰ mean, and how was the religion chosen?", "turns_on": "Whether choice is explained through the word's sense, proofs clarifying the religion, or divine enablement.", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q15/p1", "position": "It means choosing or selecting the purest religion for them.", "reasons": "Majāz derives it from ṣafwa, purity; Qurṭubī cites a rajaz line for the form, and Samin traces its alif through yāʾ from a root waw. Jishumī explains selection either as purifying and distinguishing it through proofs or simply as choosing Islam."}, {"id": "2:132/q15/p2", "position": "God's choosing includes establishing proofs, calling them, and enabling their acceptance.", "reasons": "Rāzī adds clear proofs and protection from other religions; Kashshāf, Nasafī and Ālūsī say God enabled them to follow the finest faith. Biqāʿī calls this mercy that spares a search; Qushayrī and Abū Ḥayyān say the announcement encourages obedience and hope of divine aid."}]}
{"id": "2:132/q16", "question": "What does لَكُمُ contribute?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q16/p1", "position": "It means 'for your sake,' without implying the religion is pure only for these addressees.", "reasons": "Samin glosses lakum as li-ajlikum; Ālūsī says Islam is inherently the purest religion, rather than only pure for them."}]}
{"id": "2:132/q17", "question": "Which religion is meant by ٱلدِّينَ?", "turns_on": "The known historical religion of Islam and an inward account of its divine unity.", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q17/p1", "position": "It is the known religion of Islam, the upright monotheist way, selected over other religions.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī says the definite article marks the religion familiar from ancestral counsel. Wāḥidī, Jishumī, Ṭabrisī, Qurṭubī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Samin take the article as referential, rather than generic. Wāḥidī calls it ḥanīfiyya; Qushayrī says legal practices may vary while monotheist foundation stays one. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 3:19 for inherited Islam; Study Quran distinguishes Islam as Muhammad's proper name and a primordial universal orientation, citing 3:19, 3:85, 5:3 and 6:125."}, {"id": "2:132/q17/p2", "position": "In an inward reading, it is the divine religion of unity with God, beyond a separate self.", "reasons": "Qāshānī reads the enjoined word as unity and says God's religion and essence are one."}]}
{"id": "2:132/q18", "question": "What does the prohibition فَلَا تَمُوتُنَّ require?", "turns_on": "How a command expressed at the involuntary event of death applies to a person's controllable religious state.", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q18/p1", "position": "Remain in Islam at every moment, so death finds one Muslim.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī, Zajjāj and many others say death is uncontrollable and its time unknown; the command therefore addresses the lifelong state. Wāḥidī and Jishumī compare 'do not let me see you here.' Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Qurṭubī and Abū Ḥayyān call it concise admonition that also warns of sudden death. Rāzī says delay may leave one outside Islam at death; Abū Ḥayyān says avoid acts that lead to that end. Kashshāf and Bayḍāwī compare 'die a martyr' and prayer conditioned on humility; the state determines the honor or worth of death."}, {"id": "2:132/q18/p2", "position": "The needed state is inward faith alone when bodily deeds are no longer possible at death.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports this proposal, based on a Prophetic supplication for living Muslims and faithful dead, but finds it unpersuasive."}, {"id": "2:132/q18/p3", "position": "An inward reading sees natural death of ignorance replaced by death to self and life through God until bodily death.", "reasons": "Qāshānī explains the injunction as remaining alive through God."}]}
{"id": "2:132/q19", "question": "What forms and usages of māt are cited?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q19/p1", "position": "Arabic uses mawta, mayta and mamāta, with related expressions for lifelessness and death.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī transmits al-Farrāʾ's forms and usages for barren land, mass death, selling livestock as against other goods, and a person with a lifeless heart."}]}
{"id": "2:132/q20", "question": "How is فَلَا تَمُوتُنَّ formed grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q20/p1", "position": "It is a prohibitive jussive with emphatic heavy nūn; a wāw is lost at the meeting of two sukūns.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās and Qurṭubī give the jussive and deletion; Samin derives it from tamūtūnanna, with the indicative nūn dropped and the ḍamma left as a trace."}]}
{"id": "2:132/q21", "question": "Why is the death command worded this way?", "turns_on": "Whether the wording is a direct prohibition of a state at death or a metaphorical negation of the person.", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q21/p1", "position": "It makes lifelong constancy urgent by presenting death's uncertain arrival and the disgrace of dying outside Islam.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī and Abū Ḥayyān stress brevity and unknown timing; Kashshāf, Bayḍāwī and Samin say the wording judges death outside faith as devoid of good. Al-Fāḍil al-Yamanī calls it metaphorically negating the person to negate a state, but Ālūsī objects that negating the person would negate all attributes."}, {"id": "2:132/q21/p2", "position": "The wording metaphorically negates the person to negate one particular state.", "reasons": "Al-Fāḍil al-Yamanī proposes this analysis; Ālūsī objects that negating a person negates all attributes, rather than just one state."}]}
{"id": "2:132/q22", "question": "What does مُسْلِمُونَ mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether Muslim describes faith and obedience generally, inward entrustment, or especially good expectation of God at death.", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q22/p1", "position": "Believers who submit obediently to God and remain sincere monotheists.", "reasons": "Muqātil explains 'submit' as sincerity. Thaʿlabī, Jishumī, Baghawī and Qurṭubī transmit variants 'believers,' 'sincere,' or 'entrusting themselves to God'; Biqāʿī says wholly surrendered. Wāḥidī reports Ibn ʿAbbās's uncompromising rejection of associating anything with God, even under torture."}, {"id": "2:132/q22/p2", "position": "It means entrusting oneself to God's command at all times.", "reasons": "Tustarī says continuous surrender and entrustment distinguish those who follow divine command from those left to reasoning; the wording admits a particular or general sense."}, {"id": "2:132/q22/p3", "position": "It includes having a good opinion or hope of one's Lord at death.", "reasons": "Al-Fuḍayl b. ʿIyāḍ gives this gloss. Baghawī cites Jābir's report that the Prophet said three days before death that none should die without good opinion of God; Qurṭubī includes good hope among glosses."}]}
{"id": "2:132/q23", "question": "What is the grammatical function of وَأَنتُم مُّسْلِمُونَ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q23/p1", "position": "It is a nominal subject-predicate clause in the circumstantial accusative, within an exception of states.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Qurṭubī state the circumstantial analysis; Samin calls it a total exception of states governed by the preceding verb."}]}
{"id": "2:132/q24", "question": "What does the verse teach about final states and human action?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q24/p1", "position": "Steadfast practice and intention seek a Muslim end; deeds are judged by their endings.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr says people generally die and rise in the condition they followed, and God eases good intentions; he reconciles a sound final-destiny hadith by versions saying contrary deeds only appeared so to people and cites 92:5–10. Abū Ḥayyān explicitly cites the judgment of deeds by endings. Tustarī says piety is required according to capacity under 3:102 and is no license to abandon it."}, {"id": "2:132/q24/p2", "position": "The verse indicates the prophets' faithful descendants and divine selection are fitting to protected prophets.", "reasons": "Jishumī says Abraham accepted truth when clear, resisted habit and desire, and was chosen for obeying well; the verse indicates prophetic protection from sin and that descendants followed Islam."}]}
{"id": "2:132/q25", "question": "What inward or spiritual lessons are drawn from the testament?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q25/p1", "position": "Surrender calls for entrusting oneself to God, dying to self, and inward piety that transforms outward life.", "reasons": "Sulamī links Abraham's charge to his unhesitating submission during his son's sacrifice until ransom. Tustarī reports that reforming the inward reforms the outward; Godfearing people become mercy for wrongdoers, and 49:13 promises honor, nearness, Paradise and success through piety. Qāshānī reads Islam as unity and life through God."}]}

 "Ṭabrisī states the lesson. Al-Ḥasan says Jacob had no bequest but piety, implying deathbed testament. Ibn ʿĀshūr says counsel is given when loss is feared, especially death or departure. Abū Ḥayyān cites the Prophet's challenge to a father who gifted only one child and wanted equal dutifulness."}, {"id": "2:132/q26/p2", "position": "A testament may also be delivered before another feared loss of religious teaching.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the fathers may have spoken at death, as 2:133 suggests, or at another time."}]}
{"id": "2:132/q27", "question": "What occasion or challenge is reported for the verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q27/p1", "position": "It answered Jews who claimed Jacob enjoined Judaism on his sons at death.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī transmits this report; Biqāʿī links the following verses to refuting Jewish and Christian claims that the patriarchs followed their later religions."}]}
{"id": "2:132/q28", "question": "How does this verse connect with its surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q28/p1", "position": "It continues the account of Abraham's submission and care for descendants, then presents the religion transmitted through Jacob against later scriptural claims.", "reasons": "Jishumī says the sequence moves from concern and prayers for descendants' welfare to religion. Biqāʿī places the testament after Abraham's leadership and before refutation of later Jewish and Christian identifications. Abū Ḥayyān says the prophets' call continues and praises the discourse's coherence, comparing the challenge at 17:88. Elmalılı says it clarifies Israel's brothers and Islam's value; Study Quran traces submission from 2:128 onward."}, {"id": "2:132/q28/p2", "position": "The 2:133 account of Jacob's own address supports understanding him as another testator.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr explicitly adduces the next verse, and Ibn ʿĀshūr cites it as evidence for a possible deathbed setting."}]}
{"id": "2:132/q29", "question": "What other reports about Abraham's era accompany the discussion?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q29/p1", "position": "Chronologies and genealogies are reported with differing figures and textual lineages.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī transmits a prophetic report of eight thousand prophets, half from Israel. Qurṭubī and Abū Ḥayyān date Abraham's death about 2,600 years before Muhammad, while noting a Jewish chronology 400 years shorter. Biqāʿī gives the Torah lineage through Terah and Noah and notes Luke's extra Cainan."}, {"id": "2:132/q29/p2", "position": "The Torah account traces Abraham's migration, covenants, children and descendants.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī reports Terah leaving Ur for Haran, God's call to Abram at seventy-five, travel to Canaan and Egypt, Lot's separation and rescue, a star-numbered progeny and promised land, the four-hundred-year enslavement prediction, Hagar and Ishmael, Abraham's renaming and covenant at ninety-nine, circumcision, Sarah and Isaac, Ishmael's blessing and twelve princes, and Hagar's later wilderness ordeal. He gives ages eighty-six at Ishmael's birth, thirteen at his circumcision, and day eight for Isaac's. He reconciles a Torah exile account with the sound report of nursing Ishmael at the House by possible miraculous travel. He and earlier scholars read the promises about blessing through Abraham and Ishmael's hand as prophecies of Muhammad."}]}
{"id": "2:132/q30", "question": "What does the name ٱللَّهَ involve in lexical analysis?", "turns_on": "Whether the divine name is derived and what function al- has.", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q30/p1", "position": "The article replaces a deleted hamza from ilāh.", "reasons": "Al-Itqān reports Sībawayh and al-Fārisī: the article's fixed form and hamza's cut pronunciation support the analysis."}, {"id": "2:132/q30/p2", "position": "The article marks glorifying definiteness added to a form from lāh.", "reasons": "Al-Itqān reports this alternative."}, {"id": "2:132/q30/p3", "position": "The al- is inseparable from the name and is not definiteness.", "reasons": "Al-Itqān attributes this to a group."}, {"id": "2:132/q30/p4", "position": "The form grows from written hāʾ, possessive lām, and exaltatory al-.", "reasons": "Al-Itqān attributes this derivation to some."}, {"id": "2:132/q30/p5", "position": "The name is indivisible and has no prior derivation.", "reasons": "Al-Itqān attributes this to al-Khalīl and others."}]}
{"id": "2:132/q31", "question": "How are feminine and diminutive forms illustrated beside the address 'my sons'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q31/p1", "position": "Sībawayh drops an added feminine tāʾ in diminutives and substitutes original feminine hāʾ; some Arabic usage varies.", "reasons": "He exemplifies bint → bunayya and ukht → ukhayya; other Arabs say hunayha for hunt and hunayya for hun, with hāʾ substituting for yāʾ as in dhih."}]}
{"id": "2:132/q32", "question": "What do comparisons of smooth and subtle expression illustrate in the accompanying material?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q32/p1", "position": "Smooth wording is clear and easy on the tongue; a subtle comparison asks the reader to infer a deeper relation.", "reasons": "Jurjānī distinguishes ordinary praise of transparent, familiar diction from a refined ring image: Kaʿb described al-Muhallab's sons as day guardians and night cavalry, united like a ring without a discernible end. The image needs discernment beyond immediate hearing."}]}
{"id": "2:132/q33", "question": "What broader remarks on Qur'anic letters accompany the material?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q33/p1", "position": "Common opening letters can represent the whole and carry articulatory significance.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān says alif, lām, mīm are common and span deep throat, tongue tip and closed lips; the testimony of faith similarly entails other duties. {"id": "2:132/q34", "question": "How do the accompanying recitation discussions distinguish stopping and pausing?", "turns_on": "Whether a brief sakt requires specific transmission or can clarify an ending more generally.", "positions": [{"id": "2:132/q34/p1", "position": "Verse fragments should not be left unfinished; qaṭʿ ends recitation at verse end, waqf pauses for breath and resumption, and sakt interrupts briefly without breath.", "reasons": "Al-Nashr and al-Itqān transmit Ibn Abī al-Hudhayl's report that predecessors disliked abandoning part of a verse; al-Jazarī and al-Suyūṭī infer the Companions.
